items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (By + -ing), passage-final blank; the artist is the right subject
items.passage: Malian artist Abdoulaye Konaté trained as a painter but has worked mainly with textiles since the 1990s, particularly the brightly dyed cotton fabric traditionally sold in West African marketplaces. By stitching together hundreds of individual strips of this fabric, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Konaté creates large wall hangings in which colors often shift gradually from one shade to the next.
large wall hangings in which colors often shift gradually from one shade to the next are created by Konaté.
Konaté’s large wall hangings often have colors that shift gradually from one shade to the next.
the colors in Konaté’s large wall hangings often shift gradually from one shade to the next.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes someone who is “stitching together hundreds of individual strips of this fabric”: the artist. Choice A places “Konaté” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that Konaté is the one doing the stitching.

B.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
B.why_wrong: “Large wall hangings” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the wall hangings stitched together the strips of fabric.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “Konaté’s large wall hangings,” not Konaté, so the sentence illogically says that the wall hangings stitched together the strips of fabric.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the colors
D.why_wrong: “The colors” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that colors stitched together the strips of fabric.

items.notes: Subject: Abdoulaye Konaté’s textile hangings (arts, textiles). Real artist; facts kept general (trained as a painter, turned to dyed cotton textiles in the 1990s, color gradations). Band 6 as 188f7e3c (3.18): plain agent key after a By + gerund opener, passage-final blank; recipes V, P, W (no it-cleft). Key neither the longest nor the shortest option.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English

band7.why: Plan band 6. Plain agent key after a By + gerund opener, as 188f7e3c; foils V, P, W.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener (Curling away from the trunk ...), passage-final blank; the right subject is a part of the thing (its outer bark), not the thing
items.passage: Eucalyptus deglupta, a tall tree native to rainforests from New Guinea to the southern Philippines, is often called the rainbow eucalyptus. Curling away from the trunk in thin vertical strips at irregular intervals, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the rainbow eucalyptus sheds its outer bark, revealing patches of bright green that darken over months to blue and purple.
the shedding of the rainbow eucalyptus’s outer bark reveals patches of bright green that darken over months to blue and purple.
patches of bright green inner bark are revealed on the rainbow eucalyptus, darkening over months to blue and purple.
the outer bark of the rainbow eucalyptus reveals bright green inner bark that darkens over months to blue and purple.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Curling away from the trunk in thin vertical strips at irregular intervals,” describes the tree’s outer bark, not the tree itself. Choice D places “the outer bark of the rainbow eucalyptus” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the outer bark is what curls away from the trunk.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun, the tree
A.why_wrong: “The rainbow eucalyptus” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the tree itself, rather than its outer bark, is curling away from its own trunk in thin vertical strips.

B.recipe: nominalised subject (N) built on the right noun
B.why_wrong: The subject is “the shedding,” so the sentence illogically says that a shedding is curling away from the trunk; the outer bark appears only inside the phrase that follows “of.”

C.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
C.why_wrong: “Patches of bright green inner bark” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the newly revealed inner bark is what curls away from the trunk.

items.notes: Subject: rainbow eucalyptus (Eucalyptus deglupta) bark (science, botany). No named people. Band 7 on the 2bca654a (3.21) frame (passage-final blank after an -ing opener) with the property-key move of 2dd1b8bf; not the compound-subject architecture of w3b2_03.
band7_moves: property key (band-7 file, section 3 move 7, as 2dd1b8bf): the opener (“Curling away from the trunk”) can describe only a part of the tree, never the tree, so the right subject is “the outer bark of the rainbow eucalyptus” and the strongest foil starts with the obvious noun, the tree
the tree foil (A) keeps every fact and even says the tree sheds its outer bark, so it reads as the natural continuation
the N foil (B) contains the right noun, outer bark, but only inside an “of” phrase
no it-cleft; all four options are full, equally grammatical clauses of 18 to 21 words; the key is neither the longest nor the shortest

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English
review.note: A (the tree as subject) is wrong by the 2dd1b8bf standard (thing vs its part).

band7.why: Property-key move of 2dd1b8bf: the right subject is a part of the obvious noun (the outer bark of the tree), and the obvious noun (A) is the natural reading, wrong by the same standard CB applies to "silica glass" vs "silica glass’s atomic arrangement"; nominalised and passive foils as CB. Caveats: options run 19 to 21 words (recipe 12 to 16, not a separator per section 6) and no expletive foil.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Built of ...), mid-sentence blank; the structure is the right subject, not its builders
items.passage: Agriculture in the ancient kingdom of Saba, in present-day Yemen, depended on the torrential floods that surged down the Wadi Dhana after seasonal rains. Built of compacted earth and precisely cut stone, ______ diverted these floodwaters into irrigation channels on both sides of the valley for well over a millennium.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the Sabaeans erected a dam at Marib, more than half a kilometer long, that
the Great Dam of Marib, an embankment more than half a kilometer long,
when the Sabaeans erected a dam more than half a kilometer long at Marib, it
there was a dam more than half a kilometer long at Marib that
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something “Built of compacted earth and precisely cut stone”: the dam. Choice B places “the Great Dam of Marib” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the dam, not the people who built it, was made of earth and stone.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the builders
A.why_wrong: “The Sabaeans” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the Sabaeans themselves were built of earth and stone.

C.why_wrong: The clause beginning with “when” follows the phrase, and its subject is “the Sabaeans,” so the sentence illogically suggests that the Sabaeans were built of earth and stone.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: the Great Dam of Marib, kingdom of Saba (history, engineering). No named people; facts kept general (earth and stone, over half a kilometer long, used for more than a thousand years). Band 6 as f0864217 (3.1) and b369d54c: mid-sentence blank, the structure is the right subject and its builders the main wrong subject; recipes W, S, E.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English

band7.why: Plan band 6. Structure vs its builders, as f0864217 and b369d54c; foils W, S, E.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, passage-final blank; the novel is the right subject, and the hardest foil starts with its title
items.passage: Kamala Markandaya emigrated from India to England in 1948, but nearly all of her novels depict Indian characters and settings. A first-person account by a tenant farmer’s wife whose household endures drought, insurmountable debt, and the encroachment of a tannery on her village, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Markandaya took the title of her first novel, Nectar in a Sieve (1954), from a poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge.
the title of Markandaya’s first novel, Nectar in a Sieve (1954), comes from a poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge.
Markandaya’s first novel, Nectar in a Sieve (1954), takes its title from a poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge.
a poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge supplied the title of Markandaya’s first novel, Nectar in a Sieve (1954).
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “A first-person account by a tenant farmer’s wife,” describes a novel. Choice C places “Markandaya’s first novel, Nectar in a Sieve (1954),” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the novel is that first-person account.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the author
A.why_wrong: “Markandaya” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the author herself is a first-person account by a farmer’s wife.

B.recipe: noun one level off (N): the title, not the novel
B.why_wrong: “The title” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the novel’s title, rather than the novel, is a first-person account of the family’s hardships.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the poem
D.why_wrong: “A poem by Samuel Taylor Coleridge” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that Coleridge’s poem is the account by the farmer’s wife.

items.notes: Subject: Kamala Markandaya, Nectar in a Sieve (1954), title from Coleridge’s “Work Without Hope” (literature). The plan cell asked for band 7, but R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md, section 5), so it is written as a strong band 6 and band_target is 6. Passage-final blank as 3.12; key is the novel (possessive + title) as 5b8f9cf2 (3.7); the hardest foil (B) starts with “the title of” the novel, a noun one level off; recipes W (author), N (title), W (poem).

fixes: passage: "a tannery on their village" had a plural pronoun with the singular antecedent "household"; now "on her village" (an FSS passage must be clean outside the tested slot)
review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (band7 appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 as 5b8f9cf2, with the near-miss foil "the title of" the novel.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid with a generic plural possessor (no article)
items.passage: Engineers investigating how cats clean themselves during the many hours they spend grooming discovered that ______ hundreds of minuscule, backward-curving spines whose hollow tips transport saliva through the fur to the skin below.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage is about “cats” in general, so the plural possessive “cats’” is needed to show that the tongues belong to cats. The plain plural “tongues” is correct because nothing belongs to the tongues.

B.why_wrong: The singular possessive “cat’s” refers to one cat and would need a word such as “a” before it; the passage is about cats in general, which calls for the plural possessive “cats’.”

C.why_wrong: The tongues belong to the cats, so the plural possessive “cats’” is needed, not the plain plural “cats.”

D.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
D.why_wrong: Nothing belongs to the tongues, so the plain plural “tongues” is needed, not the possessive “tongue’s.”

items.notes: Subject: hollow spines (papillae) on cats’ tongues wicking saliva (science, biomechanics). No named researchers. Band 6 on 2784cbaf (3.24): generic plural possessor with no article (“cats’”), cued by the plural “cats” earlier in the sentence; the singular “cat’s” lacks the article it would need. Slot order differs from 3.24 and from w3b2_06 (possessor first, then the plural noun and its verb).

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English

band7.why: Plan band 6. The only R6_grid official (2784cbaf) is band 7, but here the possessor opens the clause and "cats" cues the number earlier in the sentence, simpler than 2784cbaf.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a dash-enclosed description that holds its own finite verbs
items.passage: The early Irish legal texts known as the Brehon laws—which set compensation for injuries, regulated beekeeping, and defined the duties of foster parents—______ influential across much of Ireland until the early seventeenth century, when English common law gradually replaced them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “The early Irish legal texts known as the Brehon laws.” The verbs inside the dashes (“set,” “regulated,” and “defined”) belong to the clause beginning with “which,” so the sentence still needs a finite main verb for its subject, and the past tense verb “remained” supplies it.

A.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: The participle “remaining” doesn’t supply the main clause with a finite verb, so the sentence has a subject, “The early Irish legal texts known as the Brehon laws,” but no main verb.

C.recipe: by + -ing where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The phrase “by remaining” doesn’t supply the main clause with a finite verb, so the sentence is left without a main verb.

D.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: The participle “having remained” doesn’t supply the main clause with a finite verb, so the sentence is left without a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: Brehon law, early Irish legal texts with rules on injuries, beekeeping and fosterage (social science, law). The plan cell asked for band 7, but R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items, so it is written as a strong band 6 and band_target is 6, on a75d5984 (3.13): subject + a dash-enclosed description whose own finite verbs (set, regulated, defined) can pass for the main verb; option set as 3.13 (V-ed, V-ing, by V-ing, having V-ed).

fixes: explanation and A why_wrong named the subject as "the Brehon laws"; the subject is "The early Irish legal texts known as the Brehon laws" (head "texts"); explanation now says the dash verbs belong to the which clause
review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items (band7 appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 as a75d5984, with dash-enclosed finite verbs that can pass for the main verb and 15 words after the blank.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose to-infinitive after a compound predicate (three nonfinite or finite foils)
items.passage: A six-sided jet stream, first identified in photographs taken by the Voyager probes in the early 1980s, circles Saturn’s north pole. Planetary scientists compared those images with later ones from the Cassini spacecraft and simulated the circulation of the planet’s upper atmosphere ______ why the pattern has persisted for decades.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence already has a subject (“Planetary scientists”) and two finite verbs (“compared” and “simulated”). The to-infinitive “to investigate” correctly begins a phrase that explains why the scientists compared the images and simulated the atmosphere’s circulation.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, the participle “investigating” attaches to “the planet’s upper atmosphere,” illogically suggesting that the atmosphere was investigating the pattern.

B.why_wrong: Without a conjunction such as “and” before it, the finite past tense verb “investigated” can’t be added to the scientists’ actions (“compared” and “simulated”) in this way.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, the participle “having investigated” attaches to “the planet’s upper atmosphere,” illogically suggesting that the atmosphere had investigated the pattern; it also places the investigating before the work it was meant to explain.

items.notes: Subject: Saturn’s polar hexagon, Voyager and Cassini images (science, planetary science). No named researchers. The plan cell asked for band 7, but R2_to_inf has no band-7 official items, so it is written as a strong band 6 and band_target is 6, on 512f0ac9 (3.19): purpose infinitive after a compound predicate; the noun before the blank (“atmosphere”) makes the bare -ing reading absurd. Option set varies 3.19’s: “having investigated” replaces “and V-ing,” which three earlier items of ours used.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English
review.note: A (bare "investigating" with no comma) is the slot CB marks wrong with "forging" in 512f0ac9.

band7.why: R2_to_inf has no band-7 official items (band7 appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 as 512f0ac9 (compound predicate, bare -ing foil without a comma, which CB marks wrong with "forging").

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: object pronoun with a plural rival noun (“rays”) just before the blank
items.passage: Observers watching the Sun set over a cloudless ocean horizon occasionally glimpse a brief flash of green light at the top of the disappearing solar disk. This phenomenon occurs because Earth’s atmosphere refracts, or bends, the Sun’s rays as they pass through ______, separating their colors slightly as a weak prism would.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to what the Sun’s rays pass through: “Earth’s atmosphere.” The singular pronoun “it” agrees in number with this singular antecedent.

A.recipe: wrong-number pronoun matching the nearby plural noun
A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “them” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “Earth’s atmosphere”; it would illogically say that the rays pass through themselves.

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “those” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “Earth’s atmosphere.”

C.why_wrong: The pronoun “one” is unclear here: it suggests one of several unnamed things rather than the specific atmosphere the sentence has just named.

items.notes: Subject: the green flash at sunset, atmospheric refraction (science, optics). No named people. Medium rival noun as 2.15 (plural “rays” right before the blank, after the singular antecedent “atmosphere”).

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: partial 2 x 2 grid (singular possessor + plural noun)
items.passage: Tynwald, the parliament of the Isle of Man, normally meets in the island’s capital, Douglas. Each July, however, the ______ convene for a ceremonial open-air sitting on Tynwald Hill, in the village of St John’s, where summaries of newly enacted laws are read aloud to the public.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The singular possessive “parliament’s” is correct because the two branches belong to one parliament, Tynwald. The plural noun “branches” is correct because nothing belongs to the branches in this sentence.

A.why_wrong: The branches belong to the parliament, so the singular possessive “parliament’s” is needed, not the plural noun “parliaments.”

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: Nothing belongs to the branches, so the plural noun “branches” is needed, not the possessive “branch’s.”

D.recipe: wrong possessor number and needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: The passage describes one parliament, so the plural possessive “parliaments’” is incorrect, and nothing belongs to the branches, so “branches’” is incorrect too.

items.notes: Subject: Tynwald, the Isle of Man parliament, and its open-air Tynwald Day sitting (history, government). Number cue for the possessor: “Tynwald, the parliament” (one parliament). Grid as 2.24 (one distractor wrong in both slots).

fixes: first sentence (world’s oldest legislature, Norse assemblies, tenth century) echoed official 2b6e1c06 (the Althing); rewritten around the Douglas chamber and the St John’s sitting; number cue "the parliament" kept
review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (“mantle”) behind an appositive full of plural nouns
items.passage: Giant clams, the largest living bivalves, harbor colonies of photosynthetic algae within their tissues. The mantle of each clam, a fleshy layer that extends beyond the edges of its shell and contains millions of these microscopic algae, ______ frequently patterned in iridescent shades of blue, green, and gold.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “mantle” (“The mantle of each clam”), so it takes the singular verb “is.” The plural nouns inside the phrase set off by commas, such as “edges” and “algae,” only describe the mantle.

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “mantle.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “mantle.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “mantle.”

items.notes: Subject: giant clam mantles hosting photosynthetic algae (science, marine biology). No named people. Medium attractors as 2.21: plural nouns (edges, millions, algae) inside the appositive between head and blank.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: compound subject with “each” phrase holding singular nouns
items.passage: Economists generally expect consumers to purchase less of a product as its price rises. Veblen goods and Giffen goods, each named for the economist associated with it, ______ notable exceptions: demand for certain luxury items can increase alongside their price, and so can demand for some inexpensive staple foods.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the compound “Veblen goods and Giffen goods,” which is plural, so it takes the plural verb “are.” The phrase “each named for the economist associated with it” describes the two kinds of goods; its singular words don’t change the number of the subject.

A.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” doesn’t agree with the plural compound subject “Veblen goods and Giffen goods.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” doesn’t agree with the plural compound subject “Veblen goods and Giffen goods.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” doesn’t agree with the plural compound subject “Veblen goods and Giffen goods.”

items.notes: Subject: Veblen and Giffen goods as exceptions to the law of demand (social science, economics). No study details. Frame as 2.13: compound subject followed by an “each” phrase whose singular nouns (economist, it) tempt a singular verb.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; exactly one grammatical in standard written English

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener (A calligrapher who ...), mid-sentence blank; the person is the right subject
items.passage: A calligrapher who trained in Baghdad before settling in Paris in 1969, ______ poets and philosophers from many different cultures and eras in broad, sweeping strokes of colored ink.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the work of Hassan Massoudy often renders the words of
it is Hassan Massoudy who often renders the words of
Hassan Massoudy’s brush often renders the words of
Hassan Massoudy often renders the words of
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “A calligrapher who trained in Baghdad before settling in Paris in 1969,” describes a person. Choice D places “Hassan Massoudy” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that Massoudy is that calligrapher.

A.why_wrong: “The work of Hassan Massoudy” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that Massoudy’s work is a calligrapher who trained in Baghdad.

B.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “Hassan Massoudy’s brush,” not Massoudy, so the sentence illogically says that a brush trained in Baghdad and settled in Paris.

items.notes: Subject: Hassan Massoudy, Iraqi-born calligrapher in Paris since 1969 (arts, calligraphy). Real artist; facts kept general. Medium as 2.10: person as the right subject after a noun-phrase opener, mid-sentence blank; recipes N, E, P.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: subject pronoun for a named person

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent, the artist Twins Seven-Seven.

C.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “those” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent, the artist Twins Seven-Seven.

B.why_wrong: “Bearing” is not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.

C.why_wrong: “To bear” is not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.

A.why_wrong: “Rushed” is the past tense, but the text describes an event that still happens every six hours.

B.recipe: past perfect where the present is needed
B.why_wrong: “Had rushed” describes an action completed before another past action, which does not fit a repeated present event.

C.why_wrong: “Will have rushed” describes an action completed by a future time, which does not fit an event that happens every six hours.

items.notes: Subject: the Saltstraumen tidal current near Bodø, Norway (science, earth science). B.why_wrong: “Will remain” describes the future, but the hiding ended in 1994.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Despite being ...), mid-sentence blank; the right subject is a possessive noun phrase built on the obvious noun (the city’s gold leaf)
items.passage: Kanazawa, Japan, manufactures nearly all of the country’s gold leaf, which artisans produce by repeatedly hammering gold between sheets of specially treated paper. Despite being hundreds of times thinner than a human hair, ______ years of exposure to sunlight and rainfall on the exteriors of temples and shrines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the city produces gold leaf that is sturdy enough to withstand
the city’s gold leaf is sturdy enough to withstand
it is the city’s gold leaf that is sturdy enough to withstand
the gold leaf’s sturdiness allows it to withstand
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Despite being hundreds of times thinner than a human hair,” describes something extremely thin: the gold leaf. Choice B places “the city’s gold leaf” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the gold leaf, though thin, is sturdy enough to withstand years of sunlight and rainfall. The possessive “the city’s” only tells whose gold leaf it is; the subject is “gold leaf.”

A.why_wrong: The subject is “the city,” so the sentence illogically says that the city is hundreds of times thinner than a human hair.

C.why_wrong: The sentence begins with “it is,” so the opening phrase has nothing to describe; “the city’s gold leaf” appears only inside the “it is ... that” frame.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the gold leaf’s sturdiness,” not the gold leaf, so the sentence illogically says that sturdiness is hundreds of times thinner than a human hair.

items.notes: Subject: Kanazawa gold leaf (arts and crafts). Facts kept general and known (Kanazawa makes nearly all of Japan’s gold leaf, beaten between treated paper to about 0.1 micrometer, several hundred times thinner than a hair; used on temple exteriors). Band 7 as 37e5c794 (3.16, the only band-7 prep-gerund official): property opener (Despite being + thickness), right subject a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (band7 section 3.7: 3 of 5 band-7 R3 keys work this way), W uses that obvious noun (the city), E carries the key’s own noun phrase inside the cleft, P/N subject is the hammering. Reviewer: D was the artisans’ hammering (killed by one obvious fact); it is now the possessive of the obvious noun, as the P option of 37e5c794 (commercial plastics’ two associated problems), so B and D both open with a possessive built on gold leaf and the student must find the head noun.

fixes: D hardened from “the artisans’ hammering makes the leaf” (killed by one obvious fact) to the possessive of the obvious noun, “the gold leaf’s sturdiness allows it to withstand,” as 37e5c794; why_wrong and notes updated
review.note: Key seen in the first structure dump before the blind solve (blind solve compromised).
